AL.v: Alabama's large metro systems rarely record health-based violations.

AK.v: Urban Alaska systems are consistently compliant.

AZ.v: Metro utilities are reliably compliant; arsenic exceedances in small groundwater systems account for most of Arizona's health-based violations.

AR.v: Central Arkansas Water and the other metro systems rarely record health-based violations.

CA.v: Roughly 300 mostly small systems appear on California's Human Right to Water failing-systems list at any time, serving under 2% of the population.

CO.v: Front Range metro systems are consistently compliant.

CT.v: Connecticut consistently ranks among the states with the fewest health-based violations, helped by watershed-protection laws and consolidation into large professional utilities.

DE.v: Health-based violations are uncommon; Delaware's small size and consolidation into three main utilities keeps oversight tight.

DC.v: DC Water currently meets all federal health-based standards.

FL.v: Large Florida utilities are broadly compliant; disinfection byproduct exceedances in mid-size and small systems account for most health-based violations.

GA.v: Metro utilities meet health-based standards; north Georgia's carpet-belt PFAS and small-system DBPs drive most enforcement attention.

HI.v: County water systems consistently meet all federal standards.

ID.v: Boise and the larger cities are consistently compliant.

IL.v: Lake Michigan systems rarely violate standards.

IN.v: Large systems are consistently compliant; violations skew to small rural systems (nitrate, occasional bacteria) and aging industrial-city distribution.

IA.v: Public systems mostly comply because they invest in treatment: the cost of nitrate removal is the real burden.

KS.v: Wichita, Topeka, and the Johnson County systems are consistently compliant.

KY.v: Kentucky consolidated aggressively (fewer than 400 community systems remain), lifting most of the state to solid compliance.

LA.v: Compliance is solid in the metros but fragile in small systems, which lead the nation in boil-water advisories per capita.

ME.v: Public systems have strong compliance, anchored by Sebago Lake's waiver-grade quality.

MD.v: The two dominant utilities are strongly compliant; Baltimore's issues are distribution-side (breaks, pressure, aging valves) rather than treatment failures.

MA.v: Health-based violations are rare and mostly PFAS-related as the strict state standard came into force.

MI.v: The Great Lakes metro systems are consistently compliant.

MN.v: Twin Cities systems hold strong compliance records.

MS.v: Mississippi consistently ranks near the top for boil-water advisories and small-system violations per capita.

MO.v: The metro systems are reliably compliant; most violations occur in small rural systems.

MT.v: Public-system compliance is solid; most violations are monitoring lapses in very small systems.

NE.v: Omaha and Lincoln are consistently compliant.

NV.v: The metro systems are consistently compliant.

NH.v: Public systems show strong compliance, with PFAS remediation the active front.

NJ.v: Compliance among major systems is solid and state oversight is unusually strict.

NM.v: Albuquerque, Las Cruces, and Santa Fe comply fully.

NY.v: NYC's system is consistently compliant with a filtration waiver held since 1993 (UV disinfection added).

NC.v: The big Piedmont utilities are consistently compliant.

ND.v: Compliance is strong and improving as regional systems replace marginal wells; remaining violations are mostly monitoring lapses in very small systems.

OH.v: Metro systems comply consistently; the compliance frontier is bloom-season vigilance on Lake Erie and lead-line replacement.

OK.v: The metros are reliably compliant; Oklahoma's violation counts concentrate in its very large roster of small rural systems, and consolidation moves slowly.

OR.v: The big western systems comply fully.

PA.v: The major systems comply; Pittsburgh's lead exceedances ended after treatment and replacement.

RI.v: The Scituate supply itself is excellent; compliance attention centers on Providence's lead plumbing rather than source or treatment failures.

SD.v: Compliance is solid, strengthened as Lewis & Clark pipeline water replaces marginal local wells; remaining violations are small-system nitrate and monitoring lapses.

TN.v: The four metro systems are consistently compliant, and Memphis' aquifer needs minimal treatment.

TX.v: Metro systems are reliably compliant; Texas' violation totals lead the nation mostly because its small-system count does.

UT.v: Wasatch Front systems are consistently compliant.

VA.v: The large systems comply consistently; Richmond's 2025 outage was an infrastructure failure rather than a standards violation and accelerated state scrutiny of plant resilience.

WA.v: Metro compliance is excellent, and Seattle holds filtration avoidance for the Cedar supply.

WV.v: The large WVAW systems meet standards; small coalfield systems generate chronic violations and outages, and several have been taken over or regionalized.

c: Nitrate and bacteria in karst wells
WI.v: Milwaukee and Madison hold strong records; violations concentrate in karst-country wells (largely private, outside SDWA), small-system radium, and PFAS-affected wells.

WY.v: Large-system compliance is solid; the state's violation profile is dominated by monitoring lapses and radionuclide exceedances in very small systems, often resolved by new wells or hookups to regional supply.
